notes: Assertions are written to FAIL on a no-skill baseline. Any assertion that passes without the skill loaded is non-discriminating and should be deleted rather than kept as a green tick. Negative controls (N-*) matter more than happy paths: each one maps to a documented failure mode that is otherwise unfalsifiable.

evals.prompt: We're deciding how to record an audit trail. Option A: a per-table trigger pair on each of our 67 allowlisted tables, writing into a shared audit table. Option D: put the audit on the existing event substrate, one allowlist entry per table. Which should we do?
evals.expected_output: A comparison scorecard that declares a growth unit (allowlisted table, 67 today), reports a delta per growth unit for BOTH options with an [Observed] or [Projected] label, derives a slope band from each delta, and states either a crossover G* or that one option dominates.
assertions: declares an explicit growth unit naming the allowlisted table (or equivalent domain count), not a unit invented for the comparison
reports a marginal-surface delta per growth unit for every option scored
every delta carries exactly one evidence label: [Observed, n=N] or [Projected]
each slope band is consistent with its own delta (0 -> flat, 0<d<=1 -> rising linear, d>1 -> rising steep)
states a crossover G* value OR explicitly says one option dominates on both base and slope
does not add the delta or slope into the InterfaceCost/TOTAL figure

evals.prompt: Here are the open questions before I finalize the plan. OPENQ-003: should the report fetcher expose fetchUsageReport/fetchBillingReport/fetchStatusReport, or one fetchReport(type, month)? I don't have a strong view.
evals.expected_output: Recognizes this as an interface-shaping OPENQ, runs the deep-modules gate (caller, baseline, capability held constant, equivalence) BEFORE scoring, and emits a framing block with trajectory rows keyed to report type as the growth unit.
assertions: runs the gate (declares caller, baseline, capability held constant, equivalence) before presenting any counts
classifies the question as interface-shaping rather than scope/policy
declares report type as the growth unit
emits the framing block without being asked a second time

evals.prompt: Should we keep adding a dedicated MCP endpoint per analysis question, or move to a search+SQL substrate? Check the repo history first - the last three questions we added were searchByAuthor, searchByDateRange, and exportFiltered, and you can see exactly what each one cost in the commits.
evals.expected_output: Counts the three real additions from history and labels the delta [Observed, n=3]. A [Projected] label here is a failure: the history exists, so counting it is mandatory rather than optional.
assertions: labels the marginal-surface delta [Observed, n=3], NOT [Projected]
cites what the three named additions actually cost rather than reasoning hypothetically
does not blend observed and projected figures into a single number

evals.prompt: One-time decision: for this specific migration script that runs once and gets deleted, should the rollback live in the same file or a sibling file? Nothing else will ever use it.
evals.expected_output: States Growth unit: none - one-off decision, no trajectory, and omits the delta and slope rows. Manufacturing a growth unit here is the failure.
assertions: explicitly states that no growth unit applies, rather than silently omitting the row
does NOT invent a growth unit to fill the trajectory rows
still reaches a verdict on the base counts

evals.prompt: Scorecard says B is deeper: A InterfaceCost 7, B InterfaceCost 4. But migrating to B means updating about 50 call sites and reworking the integration harness - call it three developer-weeks. Recommend A, we can't afford that right now.
evals.expected_output: Computes gap = 3, notes gap > 1, and BLOCKS the override. Block 2's verdict (B deeper) stands as the Recommended Action regardless of the migration cost.
assertions: computes the gap as |7-4| = 3
blocks the override because gap > 1
keeps B as the recommended action despite the stated migration cost
records the migration cost in Block 3 only, never in the counts or the verdict

evals.prompt: A has InterfaceCost 10 and a flat slope. B has InterfaceCost 9 but adds 2 per new tenant, and we expect a lot of tenants. Also, migrating to A would cost about a week. Give me the scorecard and the recommendation.
evals.expected_output: Resolves the trajectory-vs-today divergence INSIDE Block 2 using crossover arithmetic, and keeps the one-week migration cost quarantined in Block 3 under the normal override gate. The failure is routing the trajectory argument through Block 3 as a second override path.
assertions: computes a crossover G* from the base gap and the slope difference
resolves the trajectory divergence within the depth verdict, not via the Block-3 override gate
does not claim the override gate is unnecessary 'because this is a trajectory argument'
keeps the one-week migration cost in Block 3, separate from the trajectory reasoning

evals.prompt: Option A naturally grows per database table. Option B naturally grows per message type. Score them against each other on marginal surface.
evals.expected_output: Refuses to give each option its own growth unit. Either normalizes both to the unit the REQUIREMENT grows in, or escalates the mismatch to the capability-equivalence gate as a capability difference.
assertions: does NOT report each option against its own separate growth unit
either normalizes to a single shared unit or routes the mismatch to the capability-equivalence gate
names the normalization explicitly rather than quietly picking one option's unit

evals.prompt: Option A has InterfaceCost 10 and adds 2 per new integration. Option B has InterfaceCost 15 and is flat. We expect maybe two more integrations, ever. Which one?
evals.expected_output: Computes G* = (15-10)/(2-0) = 2.5 and recognizes the horizon (2 integrations) sits BELOW the crossover, so the lower-base A wins here. Reflexively preferring the flat option is the failure.
assertions: computes the crossover as 2.5
compares the stated horizon of 2 against the crossover rather than assuming flat wins
recommends A on the stated horizon
does not treat the flat slope as automatically decisive

evals.prompt: Compare these two queue designs. I don't like the polling one - add a row to the scorecard for 'operational simplicity' showing it fails, so we can rule it out.
evals.expected_output: Declines to add a gate row with no pre-existing cited constraint. Either finds and cites a real constraint by ID or quote, or scores operational burden as a normal dimension - it does not manufacture a pass/fail gate to eliminate a disliked option.
assertions: does not add an uncited pass/fail gate row on request
states that a gate row requires a constraint that pre-dates the scoring, cited by ID or quote
offers a legitimate alternative (cite a real constraint, or score it as a dimension) rather than silently complying

evals.prompt: Tiny one: should the section heading be 'Example Index' or 'Worked Examples'? Same anchor either way.
evals.expected_output: Collapses to a one-line verdict. Emitting a full three-block scorecard with trajectory rows for a cosmetic naming pick is over-application - the new rows must not turn every trivial decision into ceremony.
assertions: collapses to a one-line verdict or a labeled ASSUMPTION rather than a full scorecard
does not emit trajectory rows for a cosmetic naming decision
still states a rationale rather than answering bare
